statement: A smooth [conformal map](c:conformal-map) $F$ from a connected open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $n \ge 3$, is a [Möbius transformation](c:moebius-transformation) restricted to $U$. It has the form $p + sQx$ or $p + sQ(x - x_0)/|x - x_0|^2$, with $Q$ orthogonal, $s > 0$ and $x_0 \notin U$.

hypotheses.text: The dimension satisfies $n \ge 3$.
The set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is open and [connected](c:connected-space).
The map $F\colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth and [conformal](c:conformal-map): $DF(x)^{T} DF(x) = \lambda(x)^2 I$ with $\lambda(x) > 0$.

conclusion: On $U$, either $F(x) = p + sQx$ or $F(x) = p + sQ(x - x_0)/|x - x_0|^2$, for some $p \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $s > 0$, orthogonal $Q$ and $x_0 \notin U$.

proofs.name: Differentiating the conformal factor
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the conformality equation until $1/\lambda$ is a quadratic polynomial, then invert at its zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for $F$ of class $C^3$ or better; for $n = 2$ the statement fails, because every holomorphic map with nonzero derivative is conformal. The final step splits into constant and nonconstant $\lambda$.

roles.why: Conformality gives the orthogonality relations $F_i \cdot F_j = \lambda^2 \delta_{ij}$ that start the computation.
Three distinct indices exist only when $n \ge 3$; they give $\varphi_{ij} = \varphi_i \varphi_j$ and equal diagonal entries.
On a [connected](c:connected-space) set a function with zero gradient is constant, and the inverted domain stays connected.

steps.slogan: Express the second derivatives of $F$ through the conformal factor.
steps.detail: Write $F_i = \partial_i F$ and $\varphi = \log \lambda$. Conformality says $F_i \cdot F_j = \lambda^2 \delta_{ij}$. Differentiating this and permuting the indices (the Christoffel trick) gives $F_{ij} \cdot F_k = \lambda^2(\varphi_i \delta_{jk} + \varphi_j \delta_{ik} - \varphi_k \delta_{ij})$. The $F_k$ form an orthogonal basis of vectors of length $\lambda$, so $F_{ij} = \varphi_i F_j + \varphi_j F_i - \delta_{ij} \sum_k \varphi_k F_k$.

steps.slogan: Equate the mixed third derivatives of $F$ for several index patterns.
steps.detail:
Differentiate the formula for $F_{ij}$ and use $F_{ijl} = F_{ilj}$. For distinct $i, j, l$, which exist because $n \ge 3$, independence of $F_j$ and $F_l$ gives $\varphi_{ij} = \varphi_i \varphi_j$ for all $i 
e j$. For $i 
e l$ the equation $F_{iil} = F_{ili}$ then gives $\varphi_{ii} + \varphi_{ll} = \varphi_i^2 + \varphi_l^2 - |
abla \varphi|^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\psi = 1/\lambda$ is a quadratic polynomial.
steps.detail:
With $\psi = e^{-\varphi}$ the relations read $\psi_{ij} = 0$ for $i 
e j$ and $\psi_{ii} + \psi_{ll} = |
abla \psi|^2/\psi$ for $i 
e l$. Three indices give $\psi_{ii} = \psi_{ll} = \mu$, so the [Hessian](c:hessian) of $\psi$ is $\mu I$, and $\partial_i \mu = \partial_i \psi_{ll} = \partial_l \psi_{il} = 0$ makes $\mu = 2a$ constant. Hence $\psi = a|x|^2 + b \cdot x + c$ with $|b|^2 = 4ac$, because $|
abla \psi|^2 = 2\mu\psi$.

steps.slogan: Solve the case of constant conformal factor: $F$ is a similarity.
steps.detail: If $\lambda$ is constant on a connected open set, then $\varphi_i = 0$ and $F_{ij} = 0$, so $F(x) = p + Ax$ with $A^T A = \lambda^2 I$. Thus $A = \lambda Q$ with $Q$ orthogonal, and $F$ is a [homothety](c:homothety) followed by an orthogonal map and a translation. This covers $a = 0$, where $|b|^2 = 4ac$ forces $b = 0$ and $\lambda = 1/c$.

steps.slogan: Invert at the zero of $\psi$ to make the conformal factor constant.
steps.detail: If $a \ne 0$, then $|b|^2 = 4ac$ gives $\psi = a|x - x_0|^2$ with $x_0 = -b/2a$; since $\psi > 0$ on $U$, we get $a > 0$ and $x_0 \notin U$. For the [inversion](c:inversion) $J(y) = x_0 + y/|y|^2$, the map $G = F \circ J$ has conformal factor $\lambda(Jy)\,|y|^{-2} = (|y|^2/a)\,|y|^{-2} = 1/a$ on the connected set $J^{-1}(U)$. So $G(y) = p + a^{-1}Qy$ by the previous step, and $F(x) = p + a^{-1}Q(x - x_0)/|x - x_0|^2$.

steps.slogan: Read off the Möbius form of $F$ in both cases.
steps.detail: If $\lambda$ is constant, $F = p + \lambda Q x$ is a similarity. Otherwise $F = p + a^{-1}Q(x - x_0)/|x - x_0|^2$ is a translation, an orthogonal map, a homothety and an inversion composed. Both are [Möbius transformations](c:moebius-transformation) restricted to $U$, with $s = \lambda$ or $s = 1/a$.

concepts.c:conformal-map: Conformality gives the relations $F_i \cdot F_j = \lambda^2 \delta_{ij}$ behind every step.
concepts.c:moebius-transformation: The conclusion identifies $F$ with a similarity or an inversion composed with one.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness turns a locally constant $\mu$ and a zero Hessian into global facts.
concepts.c:hessian: The Hessian of $1/\lambda$ is a constant multiple of the identity.
concepts.c:inversion: Inversion at the zero of $1/\lambda$ makes the conformal factor constant.
concepts.c:homothety: A constant conformal factor makes $F$ a homothety up to a rigid motion.

source.note: The classical differential proof of Liouville (1850): the Christoffel identity for the metric $\lambda^2|dx|^2$ and the compatibility of third derivatives; $C^3$ smoothness suffices.

statement: Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be [open](c:open-set) and let $f\colon \Omega \to \mathbb{C}$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function). If the partial derivatives of $f$ exist at every point of $\Omega$ and satisfy the [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations), then $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $\Omega$.

hypotheses.text: The set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an [open set](c:open-set).
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $\Omega$.
The partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ exist at every point of $\Omega$ and satisfy $f_x + i f_y = 0$, the [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations).

proofs.name: Baire category and Morera
proofs.slogan: Baire's theorem makes $f$ Lipschitz on a dense open set, and Morera's theorem is extended across the exceptional closed set by the cited argument.
proofs.scope: The version with partial derivatives at every point; the variant with a countable exceptional set is another family member. The proof is an outline: steps 2 and 3 are proved in full, and step 4 rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Holomorphy is local, so every point of the [open set](c:open-set) has a disc around it to work in.
Continuity makes the sets $F_n$ closed, and Morera's theorem needs a continuous function.
The existence of the partials gives the line bounds, and the equations $f_x + i f_y = 0$ make rectangle integrals vanish.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to a statement on a small disc inside $\Omega$.
steps.detail: Holomorphy is a local property, and the hypotheses pass to every open subset. So it is enough to show that $f$ is holomorphic on each open disc $D$ with $\overline{D} \subset \Omega$.

steps.slogan: Find an open set where $f$ is Lipschitz by a Baire argument.
steps.detail: Let $F_n$ be the set of $z \in D$ with $|f(z+h) - f(z)| \le n|h|$ for real $h$ and imaginary $h$ with $|h| \le 1/n$. Each $F_n$ is closed because $f$ is continuous, and $D = \bigcup F_n$ because $f_x$ and $f_y$ exist. By Baire's theorem each disc in $D$ holds a small disc $W \subseteq F_n$, and a horizontal then a vertical step gives $|f(w) - f(z)| \le \sqrt{2}\,n\,|w - z|$ on $W$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ is holomorphic on the dense open set of such discs.
steps.detail: A Lipschitz function is absolutely continuous on horizontal and vertical segments, and its partials equal its derivatives along them. So for a rectangle $R \subset W$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\oint_{\partial R} f\,dz = i\iint_R (f_x + i f_y)\,dx\,dy = 0$. Morera's theorem makes $f$ holomorphic on $W$, hence on the union $U$ of all such sets, which is open and dense in $D$.

steps.slogan: Extend the vanishing of rectangle integrals across the exceptional closed set.
steps.detail: The set $E = D \setminus U$ is closed and nowhere dense. The cited proofs treat it with a second Baire argument on $E$, Dini-derivative estimates and Lebesgue integration along lines. They obtain $\oint_{\partial R} f\,dz = 0$ also for rectangles that meet $E$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $f$ is holomorphic on $D$ from the vanishing rectangle integrals.
steps.detail: The continuous function $f$ has zero integral over the boundary of every rectangle in $D$. Morera's theorem then makes $f$ holomorphic on $D$. Since $D$ was an arbitrary disc, $f$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$.

concepts.c:open-set: Open sets give discs on which the local argument runs.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity closes the sets $F_n$ and lets Morera's theorem apply.
concepts.c:cauchy-riemann-equations: The equations make the area integral of $f_x + i f_y$ vanish.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy on every disc is the goal and follows from Morera's theorem.

source.ref: J. D. Gray and S. A. Morris, When is a function that satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations analytic?, American Mathematical Monthly 85 (1978), 246-256; the original proofs are by H. Looman (1923) and D. Menchoff, and S. Saks, Theory of the Integral, Hafner, New York, 1937, chapter IX
source.note: Steps 2 and 3 are written out here; step 4 summarizes the exceptional-set argument that Saks and Gray and Morris carry out in full.

statement: Remove one black square and one white square from a $2m \times 2n$ chessboard, with $m, n \ge 1$. Then the remaining squares have a [domino tiling](c:domino-tiling): $2 \times 1$ dominoes that cover each remaining square exactly once.

hypotheses.text: The board has $2m$ rows and $2n$ columns with $m, n \ge 1$, and its squares are colored alternately black and white.
The two removed squares have different colors.

conclusion: The remaining squares have a [domino tiling](c:domino-tiling).

proofs.name: Gomory's closed path
proofs.slogan: A closed path through all squares alternates in color, so the two removed squares cut it into two arcs of even length.
proofs.scope: Gomory's theorem for every board with an even number of rows and columns; the $8 \times 8$ board is $m = n = 4$. The original puzzle, with two same-colored corners removed, has no tiling, because each domino covers one square of each color.

roles.why: An even number of rows and columns allows a closed path through all squares, and adjacent squares differ in color.
Squares of different colors sit an odd number of steps apart, which makes both arcs even.

steps.slogan: Build a closed path through all squares of the board.
steps.detail: Number the rows $1, \dots, 2m$ and the columns $1, \dots, 2n$. Walk along row 1, then snake through rows $2, \dots, 2m$ in columns $2, \dots, 2n$, left on even rows and right on odd rows, to $(2m, 2)$. Continue to $(2m, 1)$, go up column 1 and close at $(1, 1)$. Consecutive squares share an edge, so this is a [Hamiltonian cycle](c:hamiltonian-cycle) $s_0, \dots, s_{N-1}$ with $N = 4mn$.

steps.slogan: Show that the colors alternate along the closed path.
steps.detail: Adjacent squares have different colors, so the colors of $s_0, s_1, \dots$ alternate. Hence two squares on the path have different colors exactly when their positions differ by an odd number.

steps.slogan: Cut the closed path at the two removed squares.
steps.detail: Let the removed squares sit at positions $i < j$ on the path. Deleting them leaves two arcs: the squares strictly between positions $i$ and $j$, and the squares after $j$ together with those before $i$. An arc may be empty.

steps.slogan: Count the squares of each arc to show that the count is even.
steps.detail: The removed squares have different colors, so $j - i$ is odd. The first arc has $j - i - 1$ squares, which is even. The second arc has $N - (j - i) - 1$ squares, which is even because $N$ is even.

steps.slogan: Pair consecutive squares along each arc into dominoes.
steps.detail: In an arc with an even number of squares, group the squares in order as first with second, third with fourth, and so on. Consecutive squares share an edge, so each pair is a domino. The dominoes of both arcs cover every remaining square exactly once, which is a [domino tiling](c:domino-tiling).

concepts.c:domino-tiling: The pairs of consecutive squares are the dominoes of the tiling.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-cycle: The closed path visits every square once and cuts into two arcs.

source.note: Gomory's Hamiltonian-cycle argument for the mutilated chessboard problem, as described in the Wikipedia article on that problem.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact connected polyhedron and $f\colon X \to X$ a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map. Every map $g$ [homotopic](c:homotopy) to $f$ has at least $N(f)$ fixed points, where the Nielsen number $N(f)$ is the number of essential [fixed point classes](c:fixed-point-class) of $f$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a compact connected polyhedron.
The map $f\colon X \to X$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The map $g\colon X \to X$ is [homotopic](c:homotopy) to $f$.

conclusion: The map $g$ has at least $N(f)$ fixed points.

proofs.name: Fixed point classes and index
proofs.slogan: Split the fixed points into classes, give each class an index, and match essential classes along the homotopy.
proofs.scope: The lower bound only; Wecken's theorem, that the bound is sharp for manifolds of dimension at least 3, is another member of the family. The proof takes the fixed point index and its homotopy invariance as known.

roles.why: Compactness gives finitely many classes, and local contractibility of a polyhedron makes classes open and the index defined.
A continuous self-map has a compact fixed point set, on which classes and indices are defined.
A homotopy from $f$ to $g$ matches the essential classes of the two maps.

steps.slogan: Split the fixed points of a map into Nielsen classes.
steps.detail: Call fixed points $x, y$ of $f$ equivalent if some path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$ has $\gamma \simeq f \circ \gamma$ rel endpoints. Because $X$ is locally contractible, nearby fixed points are equivalent, so each class is open in $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$. The compact set $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$ therefore has finitely many classes, and distinct classes are disjoint.

steps.slogan: Attach a fixed point index to each class.
steps.detail: Each class $C$ has an open neighborhood in $X$ that contains no other fixed point of $f$. The [fixed point index](c:fixed-point-index) $\mathrm{ind}(f, C)$ is the index of $f$ on that neighborhood. The class is essential if its index is nonzero, and $N(f)$ is the number of essential classes.

steps.slogan: Match the essential classes of $f$ and $g$ along the homotopy.
steps.detail: Let $H\colon X \times I \to X$ be a homotopy from $f$ to $g$. Classes of $\mathrm{Fix}(H) \subseteq X \times I$ are defined by paths of the same kind; each meets level $0$ in at most one class of $f$ and level $1$ in at most one class of $g$. By homotopy invariance of the index, matched classes have equal index, so $N(f) = N(g)$.

steps.slogan: Count the fixed points of $g$ by its essential classes.
steps.detail: Distinct classes of $g$ are disjoint and nonempty, so $g$ has at least one fixed point in each essential class. Hence $g$ has at least $N(g)$ fixed points, and $N(g) = N(f)$ by the matching step.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ gives a closed set of fixed points with a defined index.
concepts.c:homotopy: A homotopy from $f$ to $g$ transports classes and keeps their indices.
concepts.c:fixed-point-class: Fixed point classes are the units that the index and the count work with.
concepts.c:fixed-point-index: The index decides which classes are essential and is invariant under homotopy.

source.note: Nielsen's classical argument, as presented in R. F. Brown, The Lefschetz Fixed Point Theorem, Scott, Foresman, 1971, and B. Jiang, Lectures on Nielsen Fixed Point Theory, Contemporary Mathematics 14, AMS, 1983.

statement: Let $X$ be a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) and $P$ a [perfect](c:perfect-subgroup) normal subgroup of $\pi_1(X)$. Then attaching 2-cells and 3-cells to $X$ gives a CW complex $X^+$ with $\pi_1(X^+) = \pi_1(X)/P$ and $H_*(X^+, X; M) = 0$ for every $\mathbb{Z}[\pi_1 X^+]$-module $M$, so $X \to X^+$ is a [homology equivalence](c:homology-equivalence) with local coefficients.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex).
The subgroup $P \trianglelefteq \pi_1(X)$ is normal and [perfect](c:perfect-subgroup): $P = [P, P]$.

conclusion: There is a CW complex $X^+ \supseteq X$, built by attaching 2-cells and 3-cells, with $\pi_1(X^+) = \pi_1(X)/P$ and $H_*(X^+, X; M) = 0$ for all $\mathbb{Z}[\pi_1 X^+]$-modules $M$.

proofs.name: Attaching 2-cells and 3-cells
proofs.slogan: Kill $P$ by 2-cells, then kill the new second homology of the cover by 3-cells, and the relative chain complex becomes acyclic.
proofs.scope: Quillen's plus construction for a perfect normal subgroup $P$; the two other constructions that carry the name are other family members. Applied to the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) of $GL(R)$ and its perfect subgroup $E(R)$, it defines higher algebraic K-theory.

roles.why: A connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) accepts cells attached along loops and spheres, and has cellular chain complexes.
Normality gives a regular cover with fundamental group $P$, and perfectness gives $H_1$ of that cover equal to zero.

steps.slogan: Attach 2-cells along loops that represent the elements of $P$.
steps.detail: For each element of $P$, attach a 2-cell to $X$ along a loop that represents it, to get $Y$. By the van Kampen theorem $\pi_1(Y) = \pi_1(X)/P =: G$, because $P$ is normal.

steps.slogan: Pass to the cover of $Y$ with deck group $G$.
steps.detail: Let $\tilde X \to X$ be the [covering space](c:covering-space) with $\pi_1(\tilde X) = P$ and deck group $G$. Every attaching loop lifts to a loop in $\tilde X$, and the lifted 2-cells kill all of $\pi_1(\tilde X)$. So the covering $\tilde Y = \tilde X \cup \{\text{lifted 2-cells}\}$ is simply connected.

steps.slogan: Show that $H_2(\tilde Y) \to H_2(\tilde Y, \tilde X)$ is onto.
steps.detail: The exact sequence of the pair has the piece $H_2(\tilde Y) \to H_2(\tilde Y, \tilde X) \to H_1(\tilde X)$, and $H_1(\tilde X) = P^{ab} = 0$ because $P$ is perfect. The module $H_2(\tilde Y, \tilde X)$ is free over $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ on the lifted 2-cells.

steps.slogan: Attach 3-cells along spheres that realize a basis of the relative module.
steps.detail: The cover $\tilde Y$ is simply connected, so the Hurewicz theorem gives $\pi_2(Y) = \pi_2(\tilde Y) = H_2(\tilde Y)$. Choose classes in $\pi_2(Y)$ that map to the basis, and attach a 3-cell to $Y$ along a map $S^2 \to Y$ for each. The result is $X^+$, and $\pi_1(X^+) = G$ because 3-cells do not change $\pi_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the relative chain complex of the cover is acyclic.
steps.detail: In the cover of $X^+$ the relative cellular complex has free $\mathbb{Z}[G]$-modules in degrees 2 and 3 only, and $\partial\colon C_3 \to C_2$ sends a basis to a basis. So it is an isomorphism, and the complex is acyclic. Tensoring with any $\mathbb{Z}[G]$-module $M$ keeps it acyclic, so $H_*(X^+, X; M) = 0$.

concepts.c:cw-complex: Cell attachments keep the space a CW complex and give cellular chains.
concepts.c:perfect-subgroup: Perfectness of $P$ makes $H_1$ of the cover vanish, which the 3-cells need.
concepts.c:homology-equivalence: The conclusion says the inclusion $X \to X^+$ is a homology equivalence.
concepts.c:covering-space: The cover with deck group $G$ turns $\pi_2$ into a $\mathbb{Z}[G]$-module.
concepts.c:classifying-space: Applied to classifying spaces, the construction defines algebraic K-theory.

source.note: Quillen's plus construction by attaching 2-cells and 3-cells, as in the section on the plus construction in Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, chapter 4.

statement: Let $M$ be a [cancellative commutative monoid](c:add-cancel-comm-monoid), written additively. Every [semilinear set](c:semilinear-set) in $M$ is a finite union of proper linear sets. A linear set is $a + \mathbb{N}w_1 + \dots + \mathbb{N}w_k$; it is proper when the periods $w_i$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{N}$.

hypotheses.text: The monoid $M$ is commutative and cancellative: $x + z = y + z$ implies $x = y$.
The set $s \subseteq M$ is [semilinear](c:semilinear-set): a finite union of linear sets.

conclusion: The set $s$ is a finite union of proper linear sets.

proofs.name: Removing dependent periods
proofs.slogan: Split a linear set with dependent periods into finitely many linear sets with one period fewer, and repeat.
proofs.scope: All semilinear sets, including the empty set and single points, which are proper with no periods. The induction runs on the number of periods of one linear set.

roles.why: A finite union of linear sets reduces the claim to one linear set.
Cancellation turns a dependence of the periods into a relation between disjoint sets of periods.

steps.slogan: Reduce to one linear set and induct on its number of periods.
steps.detail: A finite union of finite unions of proper linear sets is again such a union, so it is enough to treat one linear set $L = a + \langle t \rangle$, with $t$ a finite set of periods. Use strong induction on $|t|$. If the periods in $t$ are independent over $\mathbb{N}$, then $L$ is proper, which also covers $t = \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Extract a relation between disjoint sets of dependent periods.
steps.detail: If the periods are dependent, there are $c \ne d$ in $\mathbb{N}^t$ with $\sum c_j j = \sum d_j j$. Cancellation lets us subtract $\min(c_j, d_j)$ from both sides, so $c$ and $d$ have disjoint supports. After swapping, $c \ne 0$; fix $i$ with $c_i > 0$, so $d_i = 0$.

steps.slogan: Cover $L$ by finitely many linear sets with one period fewer.
steps.detail: Take $x = a + \sum g_j j$ in $L$. While $g_j \ge c_j$ on the support of $c$, replace $g$ by $g - c + d$; the relation keeps $x$ fixed and lowers $g_i$. At the end some $g_j < c_j$, so $x \in (a + g_j j) + \langle t \setminus \{j\} \rangle$. Hence $L$ is the union of the sets $(a + kj) + \langle t \setminus \{j\} \rangle$ with $j \in \operatorname{supp}(c)$ and $k < c_j$, and each lies in $L$.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to each of the finitely many pieces.
steps.detail: Each piece is a linear set with the periods $t \setminus \{j\}$, which is fewer than $|t|$. By induction each piece is a finite union of proper linear sets. A finite union over $j$ and $k < c_j$ of such unions is again one, so $L$ is a finite union of proper linear sets.

concepts.c:add-cancel-comm-monoid: Cancellation lets us subtract common parts from a dependence relation.
concepts.c:semilinear-set: A semilinear set is a finite union of linear sets, which reduces the claim.

source.note: mathlib reduces to one linear set with IsProperSemilinearSet.biUnion and proves IsLinearSet.isProperSemilinearSet by strong induction on the number of periods, using not_linearIndepOn_finset_iffₒₛ to get the relation and the pieces (a + k • j) +ᵥ closure (t.erase j).

statement: Let $H$ be a finite dimensional [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) over a field $k$, with antipode $S$, and let $\lambda \in H^*$ be a nonzero left integral. Then the Fourier transform $\mathcal{F}\colon H \to H^*$, $\mathcal{F}(h)(x) = \lambda(x S(h))$, is a linear isomorphism, and the left integrals of $H^*$ form the line $k\lambda$.

hypotheses.text: The [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $H$ over the field $k$ is finite dimensional, with antipode $S$.
The functional $\lambda \in H^*$ is nonzero and is a left integral: $\psi\lambda = \psi(1)\lambda$ for every $\psi \in H^*$, with the convolution product.

conclusion: The map $\mathcal{F}$ is bijective, and the left integrals of $H^*$ are exactly the multiples of $\lambda$.

proofs.name: Hopf modules
proofs.slogan: Make $H^*$ a Hopf module, split it along its coinvariants, and count dimensions to see that the transform is bijective.
proofs.scope: The record names several variants of the [quantum group](c:quantum-group) Fourier transform. This proof treats the algebraic transform of a finite dimensional Hopf algebra; the analytic transforms of compact and locally compact quantum groups are other family members.

roles.why: Finite dimension gives dual bases, so a module over $H^*$ is a comodule over $H$, and dimensions can be counted.
The integral $\lambda$ spans the coinvariants, so it defines the transform.

steps.slogan: Make $H^*$ a right Hopf module over $H$.
steps.detail: Let $(e_i)$ be a basis of $H$ with dual basis $(e^i)$. Give $M = H^*$ the right action $(\varphi \cdot h)(x) = \varphi(xS(h))$ and the right [coaction](c:comodule) $\rho(\varphi) = \sum_i e^i\varphi \otimes e_i$, where $e^i\varphi$ is the convolution product. The antipode identity $S(h_{(2)})h_{(3)} = \varepsilon(h_{(2)})$ gives $\rho(\varphi \cdot h) = \rho(\varphi)\Delta(h)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the coinvariants of $M$ with the left integrals.
steps.detail: The equation $\rho(\varphi) = \varphi \otimes 1$ holds if and only if $e^i\varphi = e^i(1)\varphi$ for all $i$, that is, $\psi\varphi = \psi(1)\varphi$ for all $\psi \in H^*$. So the coinvariants $M^{\mathrm{co}H}$ are the left integrals of $H^*$.

steps.slogan: Split the Hopf module along its coinvariants.
steps.detail: For every right Hopf module $M$, the maps $m' \otimes h \mapsto m' \cdot h$ and $m \mapsto m_{(0)} \cdot S(m_{(1)}) \otimes m_{(2)}$ are inverse isomorphisms between $M^{\mathrm{co}H} \otimes H$ and $M$. Each composite is the identity by the antipode axiom $S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)} = \varepsilon(h)1$.

steps.slogan: Count dimensions to show that the left integrals form a line.
steps.detail: The isomorphism of the previous step gives $\dim H^* = \dim M^{\mathrm{co}H} \cdot \dim H$. Since $\dim H^* = \dim H \ne 0$, we get $\dim M^{\mathrm{co}H} = 1$. So the left integrals are $k\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Read the isomorphism as the Fourier transform.
steps.detail: With $\lambda$ spanning $M^{\mathrm{co}H}$, the isomorphism $k\lambda \otimes H \to M$ sends $\lambda \otimes h$ to $\lambda \cdot h$, which is the functional $x \mapsto \lambda(xS(h)) = \mathcal{F}(h)(x)$. Hence $\mathcal{F}\colon H \to H^*$ is bijective.

concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The coproduct and antipode of $H$ make $H^*$ a Hopf module.
concepts.c:quantum-group: Quantum groups carry Fourier transforms; this is the algebraic one.
concepts.c:comodule: The coaction from convolution makes $H^*$ a Hopf module with coinvariants.

source.note: The Larson-Sweedler argument through the fundamental theorem of Hopf modules (R. G. Larson and M. E. Sweedler, Amer. J. Math. 91 (1969)); the structure maps are checked here for the right Hopf module on $H^*$.

statement: Let $a, b, c, d, e \in \mathbb{C}$ with $a \ne 0$. Every root of $ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e = 0$ is an explicit expression in the coefficients that uses field operations and square roots and cube roots. Ferrari's method finds it through a [resolvent cubic](c:resolvent-cubic).

hypotheses.text: The leading coefficient satisfies $a \ne 0$.
The coefficients $a, b, c, d, e$ are complex numbers, so square roots and cube roots exist.

conclusion: Each root of the quartic is given by radicals in $a, b, c, d, e$.

proofs.name: Ferrari's resolvent cubic
proofs.slogan: Depress the quartic, complete a square with a free parameter, and choose the parameter by a resolvent cubic so that the quartic factors into two quadratics.
proofs.scope: All quartics over $\mathbb{C}$ with $a \ne 0$; the case $q = 0$ of the depressed quartic is biquadratic and is solved directly. Roots are counted with multiplicity.

roles.why: Division by $a$ and by $4a$ is needed to depress the quartic.
Over $\mathbb{C}$ the square roots and the cube roots in Cardano's formula and the quadratic formula exist.

steps.slogan: Remove the cubic term by the shift $x = y - b/(4a)$.
steps.detail: Divide by $a$ and substitute $x = y - b/(4a)$. This gives $y^4 + py^2 + qy + r = 0$, where $p, q, r$ are rational expressions in $a, b, c, d, e$.

steps.slogan: Complete a square with a free parameter $m$.
steps.detail: Write the equation as $(y^2 + p/2)^2 = -qy - r + p^2/4$. Adding $2m(y^2 + p/2) + m^2$ to both sides gives $(y^2 + p/2 + m)^2 = 2my^2 - qy + (m^2 + pm + p^2/4 - r)$.

steps.slogan: Choose $m$ so that the right side is a perfect square.
steps.detail: The right side is a perfect square in $y$ when its discriminant vanishes, that is, when $8m^3 + 8pm^2 + (2p^2 - 8r)m - q^2 = 0$. This resolvent cubic has a root $m$ given by radicals. If $q \ne 0$, then $m \ne 0$, since the cubic equals $-q^2$ at $0$; if $q = 0$ the quartic is $y^4 + py^2 + r = 0$, a quadratic in $y^2$.

steps.slogan: Factor the quartic into two quadratics by a difference of squares.
steps.detail: For $m \ne 0$ the right side equals $2m(y - q/(4m))^2$. With $\sigma = \sqrt{2m}$ the equation becomes $(y^2 + p/2 + m - \sigma(y - q/(4m)))(y^2 + p/2 + m + \sigma(y - q/(4m))) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Solve the two quadratics by the quadratic formula.
steps.detail: The four roots in $y$, with multiplicity, are the roots of the two quadratic factors, and the quadratic formula gives them by square roots. In the case $q = 0$ the same formula gives $y^2$ and then $y$. Then $x = y - b/(4a)$ gives the roots of the original equation.

concepts.c:resolvent-cubic: The resolvent cubic fixes the parameter $m$ that makes the square complete.

source.note: Ferrari's method of 1540, published by Cardano in Ars Magna (1545): depress, complete the square with a parameter, and solve the resolvent cubic.

statement: Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded open [convex set](c:convex-set), let $D$ be the open unit disk, and let $\varphi\colon \partial D \to \partial \Omega$ be a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism). Then the [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) extension $u$ of $\varphi$ to $D$ (the Poisson integral) is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) of $D$ onto $\Omega$.

hypotheses.text: The set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is bounded, open and [convex](c:convex-set).
The map $\varphi\colon \partial D \to \partial \Omega$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of the unit circle onto the boundary of $\Omega$.

conclusion: The Poisson extension $u$ of $\varphi$ is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) of $D$ onto $\Omega$, and it is continuous on $\overline{D}$ with $u = \varphi$ on $\partial D$.

proofs.name: Choquet's sign-change argument
proofs.slogan: Show that the Jacobian never vanishes by counting sign changes of a linear function of the boundary map, then use covering theory.
proofs.scope: The Radó-Kneser-Choquet theorem for convex $\Omega$; other results of Radó on harmonic functions are other family members. A convex bounded open planar set has a Jordan curve as its boundary.

roles.why: Convexity puts $u(D)$ inside $\Omega$, gives exactly two boundary points on each line through $\Omega$, and makes $\Omega$ simply connected.
The homeomorphism $\varphi$ makes the boundary values of $u$ run once around $\partial\Omega$, which gives the sign pattern and properness.

steps.slogan: Form the Poisson extension and place its values inside $\Omega$.
steps.detail: The Poisson integral $u$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) in $D$ and continuous on $\overline{D}$ with $u = \varphi$ on $\partial D$. For a linear function $\ell$, $\ell(u(z))$ is a positive-weight average of $\ell \circ \varphi$. So $u(z) \in \overline{\Omega}$, and $u(z) \in \partial\Omega$ would force $\ell \circ \varphi$ to be constant for a supporting $\ell$, which is impossible.

steps.slogan: Show that a linear function of $\varphi$ changes sign exactly twice.
steps.detail: Let $\ell$ be a nonconstant linear function and $c$ a value strictly between its minimum and maximum on $\partial\Omega$. By convexity the line $\{\ell = c\}$ meets $\partial\Omega$ in exactly two points, which cut $\partial\Omega$ into an arc in $\{\ell > c\}$ and an arc in $\{\ell < c\}$. So $\ell \circ \varphi - c$ changes sign exactly twice on $\partial D$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) of $u$ never vanishes.
steps.detail: Suppose $\det Du(z_0) = 0$. Some nonzero linear $\ell$ has $\nabla(\ell \circ u)(z_0) = 0$, so $h = \ell \circ u - \ell(u(z_0))$ is harmonic with a critical zero at $z_0$, and $h \ne 0$ because $\ell$ is not constant on $\partial\Omega$. Its zero set has at least four arcs at $z_0$, and the maximum principle keeps nodal domains from closing inside $D$, so $h$ changes sign at least four times on $\partial D$. This contradicts the previous step, because $\ell(u(z_0))$ lies strictly between the extremes of $\ell$ on $\overline\Omega$.

steps.slogan: Show that $u$ is a proper local diffeomorphism from $D$ to $\Omega$.
steps.detail: A nonvanishing Jacobian makes $u$ a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism) by the inverse function theorem. For compact $K \subset \Omega$, the set $u^{-1}(K)$ is closed in $\overline D$ and misses $\partial D$, because $u(\partial D) = \partial\Omega$. So $u^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $D$, and $u\colon D \to \Omega$ is a [proper map](c:proper-map).

steps.slogan: Conclude with covering theory that $u$ is a global diffeomorphism.
steps.detail: A proper local homeomorphism between connected locally compact Hausdorff spaces is a covering map. The set $\Omega$ is convex, hence [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space), and $D$ is connected, so the covering has one sheet. Thus $u$ is a bijective local diffeomorphism, that is, a diffeomorphism onto $\Omega$.

concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity gives two boundary points per line and a simply connected $\Omega$.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The boundary homeomorphism makes the boundary values run once around $\partial\Omega$.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: Harmonicity gives the averaging property and the maximum principle for nodal domains.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: The goal is that the extension is a diffeomorphism of $D$ onto $\Omega$.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: A nonvanishing Jacobian makes $u$ a local diffeomorphism.
concepts.c:local-diffeomorphism: A local diffeomorphism that is proper becomes a covering map.
concepts.c:proper-map: Properness lets the covering theorem apply to $u$.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: A simply connected target makes the covering a single sheet.

source.note: Choquet's argument (1945) for the Rado-Kneser-Choquet theorem, as presented in P. Duren, Harmonic Mappings in the Plane, Cambridge University Press, 2004.

statement: Let $M$ be a closed oriented connected [manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $n \ge 2$ with a transversely oriented codimension-one singular [foliation](c:foliation) $\mathcal{F}$ whose singular set is nonempty and consists of centers. Then $M$ is homeomorphic to the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$, and $\mathcal{F}$ has exactly two singularities.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a closed, oriented, connected [manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $n \ge 2$.
The manifold $M$ carries a transversely oriented codimension-one singular [foliation](c:foliation) $\mathcal{F}$ with nonempty singular set.
Every singularity of $\mathcal{F}$ is a center: near it the leaves are the level sets of a [Morse function](c:morse-function) with a local extremum there.

conclusion: The manifold $M$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$, and the foliation $\mathcal{F}$ has exactly two singular points.

proofs.name: Families of sphere leaves
proofs.slogan: Grow the sphere leaves around a center by Reeb stability until they end at a second center, then apply Reeb's theorem on two critical points.
proofs.scope: Reeb's theorem for transversely oriented singular foliations whose singularities are Morse centers, as in Reeb's original statement. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Compactness and connectedness make the family of sphere leaves exhaust $M$ and end at singularities.
The transverse orientation orders the leaves, and the leaf structure gives stability and a leaf space.
A center is a local extremum of a [Morse function](c:morse-function), so leaves near it are small spheres.

steps.slogan: Find sphere leaves around a center.
steps.detail: Near a center $p$ the leaves are the level sets of a function with a local extremum at $p$. By the Morse lemma they are small spheres $S^{n-1}$ around $p$, circles when $n = 2$.

steps.slogan: Make the family of sphere leaves open by Reeb stability.
steps.detail: A sphere leaf near $p$ has trivial holonomy, because the nearby leaves are spheres that close up. Reeb's local stability theorem then fills a neighborhood of this leaf with compact leaves diffeomorphic to the sphere.

steps.slogan: Follow the family of sphere leaves until it reaches a singularity.
steps.detail: The union of the sphere leaves in the family is open by the previous step. A regular limit leaf would again be a sphere leaf with trivial holonomy, so the family would continue; hence the family is closed in the regular set. Because $M$ is compact and connected, the leaves form an interval whose two ends are singularities $p$ and $q$, both centers.

steps.slogan: Turn the foliation into a function with exactly two critical points.
steps.detail: The transverse orientation orders the leaf space, which is an open interval, and gives a function $f\colon M \to [0, 1]$ whose level sets are the leaves. It has a minimum at $p$ and a maximum at $q$ with nondegenerate local models, and no other critical point.

steps.slogan: Apply Reeb's sphere theorem for functions with two critical points.
steps.detail: A closed manifold with a Morse function that has exactly two critical points is homeomorphic to a sphere: two balls around the extrema are glued along a boundary sphere. So $M \cong S^n$. The singularities of $\mathcal{F}$ are the critical points $p$ and $q$, so there are exactly two.

concepts.c:closed-manifold: Compactness without boundary makes the family of leaves end at singularities.
concepts.c:foliation: Leaves, holonomy and the leaf space drive the stability and extension steps.
concepts.c:sphere: The leaves are spheres, and the manifold is shown to be a sphere.
concepts.c:morse-function: Centers are Morse extrema, and the leaf coordinate is a function with two critical points.

source.ref: G. Reeb, Sur certaines propriétés topologiques des variétés feuilletées, Actualités Scientifiques et Industrielles 1183, Hermann, Paris, 1952; see also B. Scárdua and J. Seade, Codimension one foliations with Bott-Morse singularities I, Journal of Differential Geometry 83 (2009), 189-212
source.note: Scárdua and Seade prove a generalization of Reeb's theorem and obtain a Bott-Morse function $f\colon M \to [0, 1]$ whose critical set is $f^{-1}(\{0, 1\})$.

statement: Let $M$ be a closed connected orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold). Any two [Heegaard splittings](c:heegaard-splitting) of $M$ have stabilizations, obtained by adding trivial handles, that are isotopic.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a closed, connected, orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold).
The pairs $(V_1, W_1)$ and $(V_2, W_2)$ are [Heegaard splittings](c:heegaard-splitting) of $M$: each is a union of two handlebodies along their common boundary surface.

conclusion: After finitely many stabilizations of each splitting, to a common genus, the two splittings are isotopic in $M$.

proofs.name: Triangulations and stellar moves
proofs.slogan: Realize both splittings by triangulations, connect the triangulations by stellar moves, and note that each move stabilizes the splitting.
proofs.scope: Closed orientable $M$ with its piecewise linear structure, which is unique by Moise's theorem, so the statement is the same in the smooth and topological settings. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work.

roles.why: A closed 3-manifold has a triangulation, and its piecewise linear structure is unique, so any two triangulations are related by stellar moves.
Each splitting arises from a triangulation, and the induced splittings of connected triangulations become isotopic after stabilization.

steps.slogan: Attach a Heegaard splitting to each triangulation of $M$.
steps.detail: By Moise's theorem $M$ has a triangulation $T$. A regular neighborhood of the 1-skeleton is a handlebody $V_T$, and the closure of its complement is a regular neighborhood of the dual 1-skeleton, so it is a handlebody $W_T$. Thus $(V_T, W_T)$ is a Heegaard splitting.

steps.slogan: Realize each given splitting by a triangulation.
steps.detail: Singer shows that every [Heegaard splitting](c:heegaard-splitting) is isotopic to the splitting $(V_T, W_T)$ of some triangulation $T$: choose $T$ so that a spine of $V$ lies in its 1-skeleton and a spine of $W$ lies in its dual 1-skeleton.

steps.slogan: Connect two triangulations of $M$ by stellar moves.
steps.detail: Triangulations $T_1$ and $T_2$ of $M$ are piecewise linearly equivalent. By Alexander's theorem they are joined by a finite sequence of stellar subdivisions and their inverses.

steps.slogan: Show that one stellar move stabilizes the splitting.
steps.detail: A stellar subdivision of a vertex, edge, face or tetrahedron changes $(V_T, W_T)$ by adding trivial handles, up to isotopy. So along a sequence of moves, each splitting is a stabilization of its neighbor or the reverse.

steps.slogan: Join the two splittings by stabilizations of equal genus.
steps.detail: Stabilization is well defined up to isotopy, so the relation of having isotopic stabilizations is transitive. Along the chain of triangulations, the splittings of $T_1$ and $T_2$ therefore have isotopic stabilizations, and by the realization step so do the given splittings.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem concerns closed orientable 3-manifolds, which are triangulable.
concepts.c:heegaard-splitting: Splittings are the objects compared, and triangulations give a common source.

source.ref: J. Singer, Three-dimensional manifolds and their Heegaard diagrams, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 35 (1933), 88-111; K. Reidemeister, Zur dreidimensionalen Topologie, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 9 (1933), 189-194
source.note: Modern proofs by Cerf theory are in F. Laudenbach, A proof of Reidemeister-Singer's theorem by Cerf's methods, Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Toulouse 23 (2014), 197-221.

statement: Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ both contain $0$. Write $A(n) = |A \cap [1, n]|$ and $\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} A(n)/n$ for the [Schnirelmann density](c:schnirelmann-density). Then the [sumset](c:sumset) $A + B$ satisfies $\sigma(A + B) \ge \min(1, \sigma(A) + \sigma(B))$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $A$ and $B$ consist of nonnegative integers.
Both sets contain $0$.

conclusion: The density $\sigma(A + B)$ is at least $\min(1, \sigma(A) + \sigma(B))$.

proofs.name: Counting function and the missing integers
proofs.slogan: Bound the counting function of the sumset at each $n$, settling large densities by pigeonhole and the remaining integers outside the sumset by the cited argument.
proofs.scope: Mann's theorem, the sharp form of Schnirelmann's inequality $\sigma(A + B) \ge \sigma(A) + \sigma(B) - \sigma(A)\sigma(B)$. The proof is an outline: steps 1 to 3 are proved in full, and step 4 rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Only the finite parts $A \cap [0, n]$ and $B \cap [0, n]$ matter for $C(n)$.
The element $0$ puts $A$ and $B$ inside $A + B$ and adds one to each count in the pigeonhole bound.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to the counting function at a single $n$.
steps.detail: Put $C = A + B$, $\alpha = \sigma(A)$ and $\beta = \sigma(B)$. Since $\sigma(C)$ is an infimum over $n$, it is enough to show $C(n) \ge \min(n, (\alpha + \beta)n)$ for every $n \ge 1$. Only $A \cap [0, n]$ and $B \cap [0, n]$ affect $C(n)$.

steps.slogan: Settle the case $\alpha + \beta \ge 1$ by the pigeonhole principle.
steps.detail: Suppose $n \notin C$. Then $A \cap [0, n]$ and $\{n - b : b \in B \cap [0, n]\}$ are disjoint subsets of $[0, n]$, so $A(n) + B(n) + 2 \le n + 1$. But $A(n) + B(n) \ge (\alpha + \beta)n \ge n$, a contradiction. So $[1, n] \subseteq C$ and $\sigma(C) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the case $\alpha + \beta < 1$ to integers outside $C$.
steps.detail: Argue by induction on $n$ that $C(n) \ge (\alpha + \beta)n$. If $n \in C$, then $C(n) = C(n - 1) + 1 \ge (\alpha + \beta)(n - 1) + 1 \ge (\alpha + \beta)n$, because $\alpha + \beta < 1$. So only integers $n \notin C$ remain.

steps.slogan: Treat an integer $n \notin C$ by the cited argument.
steps.detail: For $n \notin C$ the cited proofs show $C(n) \ge (\alpha + \beta)n$. Mann (1942) builds on the work of Khinchin. Artin and Scherk (1943) and Dyson (1945) give other proofs, and Dyson's induction replaces the pair $(A, B)$ by a pair of the same total size whose sumset lies in $A + B$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases into the bound for every $n$.
steps.detail: For $\alpha + \beta < 1$ the induction gives $C(n) \ge (\alpha + \beta)n$ for all $n \ge 1$, and for $\alpha + \beta \ge 1$ the pigeonhole step gives $C(n) = n$. Taking the infimum over $n$ gives $\sigma(A + B) \ge \min(1, \alpha + \beta)$.

concepts.c:schnirelmann-density: The density is the infimum of $A(n)/n$, so the proof bounds each $n$.
concepts.c:sumset: The sumset $A + B$ is the set whose counting function is bounded.

source.ref: H. B. Mann, A proof of the fundamental theorem on the density of sums of sets of positive integers, Annals of Mathematics 43 (1942), 523-527
source.note: Other proofs: E. Artin and P. Scherk, On the sum of two sets of integers, Annals of Mathematics 44 (1943), 138-142; F. J. Dyson, A theorem on the densities of sets of integers, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 20 (1945), 8-14.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $N$ a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) whose order is coprime to its index $[G : N]$. Then $N$ has a complement in $G$: a subgroup $H$ with $G = NH$ and $N \cap H = 1$. So $G$ is a [semidirect product](c:semidirect-product) of $N$ and $H$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite.
The subgroup $N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
The numbers $|N|$ and $[G : N]$ are coprime.

conclusion: There is a subgroup $H \le G$ with $G = NH$ and $N \cap H = 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration does not assume that $G$ is finite; the coprimality of Nat.card N and N.index forces $N$ or its index to be trivial when one of them is infinite. Its conclusion is IsComplement' H N, which says that the product map $H \times N \to G$ is bijective.

proofs.name: Minimal counterexample and transversals
proofs.slogan: Reduce a minimal counterexample to an abelian minimal normal subgroup, then let $N$ act simply transitively on transversal classes and take a stabilizer.
proofs.scope: All finite $G$, by strong induction on $|G|$; the cases $N = 1$ and $N = G$ are trivial. The mirror statement, a complement $H$ with $G = HN$, is the same.

roles.why: Finiteness gives strong induction on $|G|$ and finite products over cosets.
Normality makes quotients $G/K$ possible and lets $G$ act on the classes of transversals.
Coprimality passes to subgroups and quotients, and makes $h \mapsto h^{[G:N]}$ a bijection of $N$.

steps.slogan: Reduce a minimal counterexample to a minimal normal subgroup $N$.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be a counterexample of least order. If $K < G$ and $KN = G$, then $N \cap K$ has a complement $H$ in $K$ by minimality, and $H$ is a complement of $N$ in $G$; so no such $K$ exists. For normal $1 < K < N$, the complement of $N/K$ in $G/K$ pulls back to $K'$ with $K'N = G$; then $K' = G$, so $N = K$. Hence $N \ne 1$ is minimal normal.

steps.slogan: Show that $N$ is an abelian $p$-group.
steps.detail: Let $p$ divide $|N|$ and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N$. By Sylow conjugacy inside $N$, $G = N \cdot N_G(P)$, so $N_G(P) = G$ by step 1 and $P$ is normal in $G$. Minimality gives $P = N$. The center $Z(N)$ is normal in $G$ and nontrivial, so $Z(N) = N$.

steps.slogan: Compare left transversals of $N$ by a difference element.
steps.detail: For left transversals $\alpha, \beta$ of $N$, let $d(\alpha, \beta) = \prod_{q \in G/N} \alpha(q)^{-1}\beta(q) \in N$. Since $N$ is abelian, $d(\alpha, \beta)d(\beta, \gamma) = d(\alpha, \gamma)$, so $\alpha \sim \beta$ iff $d(\alpha, \beta) = 1$ is an equivalence relation. Let $X$ be the set of classes; it is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Let $G$ act on the classes so that $N$ acts simply transitively.
steps.detail: Right multiplication by $g \in G$ permutes transversals and respects $\sim$, because $N$ is normal; this gives an action of $G$ on $X$. For $h \in N$, $d(\alpha, \alpha h) = h^{[G:N]}$. As $\gcd(|N|, [G:N]) = 1$, the map $h \mapsto h^{[G:N]}$ is a bijection of $N$, so $N$ acts on $X$ with trivial stabilizers and one orbit.

steps.slogan: Take a stabilizer as the complement and contradict the counterexample.
steps.detail: Fix a class $x \in X$ and let $H = \mathrm{Stab}_G(x)$. For $g \in G$, transitivity of $N$ gives $n \in N$ with $gx = nx$, so $n^{-1}g \in H$ and $G = NH$. Trivial stabilizers of $N$ give $N \cap H = 1$. So $H$ is a complement, against the choice of $G$.

concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality gives quotients and the action of $G$ on transversal classes.
concepts.c:semidirect-product: The complement makes $G$ a semidirect product of $N$ and $H$.

source.note: mathlib proves the right-complement version by a minimal counterexample (SchurZassenhausInduction.step0 to step7, with Sylow.normalizer_sup_eq_top), then the abelian case through QuotientDiff, smul_diff' and isComplement'_stabilizer_of_coprime; the left version is its mirror.

statement: Fix $A > 0$. There is a constant $c = c(A) > 0$, not effectively computable, such that $\pi(x; q, a) = \mathrm{Li}(x)/\varphi(q) + O_A\!\left(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\right)$ uniformly for $x \ge 2$, $q \le (\log x)^A$ and $\gcd(a, q) = 1$. Here $\pi(x; q, a)$ counts primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$.

hypotheses.text: The number $A > 0$ is fixed, $x \ge 2$ and the modulus satisfies $q \le (\log x)^A$.
The residue $a$ is coprime to the modulus $q$.

conclusion: The count $\pi(x; q, a)$ equals $\mathrm{Li}(x)/\varphi(q)$ up to an error $O_A\!\left(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\right)$ that is uniform in $q$ and $a$.

proofs.name: Zero-free regions and Siegel's theorem
proofs.slogan: Split the count into characters, express each as a sum over zeros, and bound the zeros by the classical region and Siegel's bound on the exceptional zero.
proofs.scope: The classical statement for moduli $q \le (\log x)^A$; the constant $c$ is ineffective because Siegel's theorem is. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited work.

roles.why: The range $q \le (\log x)^A$ makes the exceptional zero and the zero-free region give a saving $e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$.
Coprimality of $a$ and $q$ lets orthogonality of characters isolate the progression.

steps.slogan: Pass from the progression to Dirichlet characters by orthogonality.
steps.detail: Let $\psi(x; q, a) = \sum_{n \le x, n \equiv a (q)} \Lambda(n)$. Orthogonality of [Dirichlet characters](c:dirichlet-character) gives $\psi(x; q, a) = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q} \bar\chi(a)\,\psi(x, \chi)$, with $\psi(x, \chi) = \sum_{n \le x} \Lambda(n)\chi(n)$. The principal character gives the main term $x/\varphi(q)$.

steps.slogan: Write each $\psi(x, \chi)$ as a sum over zeros of $L(s, \chi)$.
steps.detail: The explicit formula, from Perron's formula and a contour shift, gives $\psi(x, \chi) = -\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho + \text{small terms}$ over the nontrivial zeros $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ of $L(s, \chi)$, plus the term $x$ for the principal character.

steps.slogan: Bound the zeros by the classical zero-free region.
steps.detail: Each $L(s, \chi)$ with $\chi \bmod q$ has no zero with $\beta > 1 - c_1/\log(q(|\gamma| + 2))$, except possibly one real zero $\beta_1$ of one real character. Inserting this into the explicit formula, as in the proof of the prime number theorem, gives $\psi(x, \chi) \ll x e^{-c_2\sqrt{\log x}}$ for $q \le (\log x)^A$, plus a term $x^{\beta_1}/\beta_1$ if $\beta_1$ exists.

steps.slogan: Bound the exceptional zero by Siegel's theorem.
steps.detail: Siegel's theorem gives $L(1, \chi) \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ for real characters, so $\beta_1 < 1 - c(\varepsilon)q^{-\varepsilon}$ with an ineffective $c(\varepsilon)$. This quantifies the nonvanishing $L(1, \chi) \ne 0$ behind Dirichlet's theorem. With $\varepsilon = 1/(2A)$ and $q \le (\log x)^A$ it gives $1 - \beta_1 \gg (\log x)^{-1/2}$, so the [Siegel zero](c:siegel-zero) term satisfies $x^{\beta_1} \ll x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$.

steps.slogan: Convert the weighted count $\psi(x; q, a)$ into the count $\pi(x; q, a)$.
steps.detail: Combining the characters gives $\psi(x; q, a) = x/\varphi(q) + O(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$ for $q \le (\log x)^A$. Partial summation removes the weight $\log p$, and prime powers contribute $O(\sqrt{x})$. This gives $\pi(x; q, a) = \mathrm{Li}(x)/\varphi(q) + O_A(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$.

concepts.c:dirichlet-character: Characters of modulus $q$ isolate the residue class $a$ by orthogonality.
concepts.c:siegel-zero: The possible real zero near $1$ is the Siegel zero, which Siegel's theorem bounds.

source.ref: H. Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory, 3rd edition, revised by H. L. Montgomery, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 74, Springer, New York, 2000
source.note: The chapters on the explicit formula, Siegel's theorem and the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions give this argument; Walfisz proved the theorem in 1936.

statement: The functor $\Omega^\infty$ is an equivalence from the $\infty$-category of [connective spectra](c:connective-spectrum) to the $\infty$-category of grouplike [symmetric monoidal $\infty$-groupoids](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-groupoid), that is, grouplike $E_\infty$-spaces. Its inverse is the delooping $B^\infty$.

hypotheses.text: The spectra are [connective](c:connective-spectrum): their negative homotopy groups vanish.
The [symmetric monoidal $\infty$-groupoids](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-groupoid) are grouplike: their set of connected components is a group.

conclusion: The functor $\Omega^\infty$ is an equivalence from connective spectra to grouplike symmetric monoidal $\infty$-groupoids, with inverse $B^\infty$.

proofs.name: Recognition of infinite loop spaces
proofs.slogan: Deloop grouplike $E_n$-spaces $n$ times for every $n$, and pass to the limit to get connective spectra.
proofs.scope: The $\infty$-categorical equivalence of Segal, Boardman-Vogt, May and Lurie; strict models are not covered. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited recognition theorems.

roles.why: Connective spectra are the limit of the tower of connected covers of pointed spaces along $\Omega$.
Grouplike structure is what allows a space to be delooped, by group completion of components.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Omega^\infty$ lands in grouplike $E_\infty$-spaces.
steps.detail: The $\infty$-category of spectra is additive, so each spectrum is canonically a commutative monoid object. The functor $\Omega^\infty$ preserves finite products, so $\Omega^\infty E$ is an $E_\infty$-space. Its set of components $\pi_0 E$ is a group, so it is grouplike.

steps.slogan: Deloop grouplike $E_n$-spaces $n$ times.
steps.detail: For group objects in spaces, $\Omega$ and $B$ are inverse equivalences between group objects and pointed connected spaces. Iterating gives May's recognition theorem: $\Omega^n$ is an equivalence from $(n-1)$-connected pointed spaces to grouplike $E_n$-spaces.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit over $n$.
steps.detail: Grouplike $E_\infty$-spaces are the limit of grouplike $E_n$-spaces, and connective spectra are the limit of the tower of $(n-1)$-connected pointed spaces along $\Omega$. The equivalences of the delooping step commute with the transition functors, so they induce an equivalence of the limits.

steps.slogan: Identify the inverse as $B^\infty$ and check the two composites.
steps.detail: The inverse is $B^\infty$, with $\Omega^\infty B^\infty X \simeq X$ for grouplike $X$. For a connective spectrum $E$ the unit map $E \to B^\infty \Omega^\infty E$ is an isomorphism on all homotopy groups, so $B^\infty\Omega^\infty E \simeq E$.

concepts.c:connective-spectrum: Connective spectra are the objects that the limit of connected covers describes.
concepts.c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-groupoid: Grouplike symmetric monoidal $\infty$-groupoids are the $E_\infty$-spaces that deloop.

source.ref: J. Lurie, Higher Algebra, preprint, September 2017, section 5.2.6 (Remark 5.2.6.26); see also J. P. May, The geometry of iterated loop spaces, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 271, Springer, 1972, and J. M. Boardman and R. M. Vogt, Homotopy invariant algebraic structures on topological spaces, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 347, Springer, 1973
source.note: The delooping step is May's recognition theorem; Lurie states the equivalence of connective spectra with grouplike E-infinity spaces in section 5.2.6.
